The Journal

Concept 1 of 4 · Direction: Editorial / journal

Evolution’s real edge over the national chains is expertise, so this concept presents the shop as a publication run by fitters. The homepage reads like a well-made print journal: a cover that sells one product (the M5 GPS DHC on a claret cover), a contents strip that states the four things the business does, then numbered features. Products appear as a listing, not a card grid, so trolleys can be compared down a single column of name, spec, price and stock, like a buyer’s guide. Typography does the work that boxes and badges do elsewhere: a heavy condensed grotesk at very large sizes against a reading serif, and black rules instead of grey hairlines.

Structural changes from the brief’s section order

The brief’s nine sections stay but are regrouped as a magazine: the hero becomes a cover plus a ‘contents’ strip that names trolleys, fitting, clubs and membership in one glance (this replaces the separate three pillar tiles). The trust row is dropped as a component; its facts (Trustpilot, dealer status, Ringwood, price promise) move into the copy where they’re relevant and into the footer colophon. Reviews become ‘Letters’; secondary categories become a typographic index.

Key components (rendered from the concept’s own CSS)

Primary action. No rounded buttons. The primary action is a full-width ink bar with an arrow, like a magazine’s call-out; secondary actions are underlined condensed links.

Imagery and photography

Large, art-directed lifestyle photography is the backbone: the fitting bay in natural light, fitters at work, trolleys on New Forest heathland (not manicured fairways). Shot documentary-style, uncropped, no posing.

Products sit as cut-outs on colour (the cover) or white (listings). Every photo has a caption, like a magazine plate.

Headline copy

H1: “Motocaddy trolleys and custom‑fitted clubs, from the people who fit them.”

Standfirst: “Free, no‑obligation fitting at our centre in Ringwood, Hampshire, and a members’ club that pays for itself on a single trolley.”

Section heads: “Why we fit for free.” · “Three makers we fit most” · “£60.90”

Motion

Almost none: arrows nudge on hover; the cover image could slowly drift on scroll (parallax under 20px). The point is stillness and confidence.

Trade-offs

Does wellThe most distinctive and premium of the four. Builds trust through expertise rather than offers; the trolley listing is genuinely useful for comparison; guides get real weight, which supports SEO.
Weaker onSlower path to purchase for someone who just wants a trolley: fewer ‘add to basket’ moments above the fold. Needs a steady stream of content and named authors to stay credible. Condensed uppercase headlines need careful copy length.
Build effortMedium. Simple components, but layouts are asymmetric and need care at every breakpoint; content editors need well-designed section blocks to keep it looking edited.
Photography neededHigh. It only works with commissioned photography (fitting bay, fitters, trolleys on course). Without it the plates look empty.
Suits bestConsidered buyers researching a £500–£1,500 trolley or a custom set; golfers who read reviews before buying.

EG monogram: Set in Archivo Condensed Black, claret ‘EG’ leading the ink wordmark in the masthead (suggestion only; the mark itself isn’t being redesigned here).
